mcqs.q: Behavior modification refers to:
opts: Structured strategies aimed at changing unhealthy habits into healthier ones
mcqs.explain: Behavior modification = structured strategies aimed at changing unhealthy habits into healthier ones; crucial for lasting compliance.

mcqs.q: ‘Compliance’ means the patient's behaviors:
mcqs.explain: Compliance = the patient's behaviors (medication, diet, lifestyle) match the provider's recommendations.

mcqs.q: ‘Non-compliance’ is best defined as:
opts: Failure or refusal to comply with prescribed treatment
mcqs.explain: Non-compliance = failure or refusal to comply, e.g. a patient who does not take a prescribed medication or follow treatment.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised CAUSE of non-compliance?
mcqs.explain: Causes include language barrier, low education, prioritising immediate pain relief, poor dentist–patient interaction, and system barriers.

mcqs.q: Which is a SYSTEM-related barrier to compliance?
opts: Complex insurance paperwork and inconvenient appointment times
mcqs.explain: System-related obstacles include financial constraints, limited access, complex administrative processes (e.g. insurance paperwork), and inconvenient times.

mcqs.q: Which is a benefit of behavior change?
opts: It improves oral health outcomes and strengthens the dentist–patient relationship
It has no effect on health
mcqs.explain: Behavior change improves oral health outcomes, prevents disease progression, enhances treatment, raises satisfaction/confidence and strengthens the relationship.

mcqs.q: Is behavior change an easy process?
opts: No — it requires effort and adopting new habits and lifestyle patterns
mcqs.explain: Behavior change is not easy; it requires effort and adopting new habits and lifestyle patterns.

mcqs.q: ‘Ambivalence’ in oral-health behavior refers to:
opts: Having mixed feelings — following the behavior some days and not others
mcqs.explain: Ambivalence = mixed/contradictory feelings about a behavior; the desire is present but barriers create resistance, so patients follow some days and not others.

mcqs.q: A child who brushes because they value a clean mouth shows which motivation?
mcqs.explain: Intrinsic motivation is driven by personal values — e.g. a child who brushes because they value a clean mouth and admire their dentist.

mcqs.q: A parent giving a sticker for brushing is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Extrinsic motivation is influenced by external rewards — e.g. a parent rewarding a child with a sticker for brushing.

mcqs.q: Habits are said to form through:
mcqs.explain: Habit formation occurs through reinforcement and repetition; positive reinforcement at recall visits encourages continued behavior.

mcqs.q: Saying "Your gums look great!" at a recall visit is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Positive reinforcement during recall visits (e.g. "Your gums look great!") encourages continued flossing.

mcqs.q: The Theory of Planned Behavior says the likelihood of following advice is shaped by attitudes, social norms, and:
mcqs.explain: The Theory of Planned Behavior: attitudes, social norms, and perceived behavioral control (confidence in one's ability).

mcqs.q: In the Theory of Planned Behavior, ‘social norms’ refers to:
opts: The patient's own belief in flossing
mcqs.explain: Social norms = e.g. family expectations about oral hygiene.

mcqs.q: ‘Perceived behavioral control’ means the patient's:
opts: Confidence in their ability to maintain a routine
mcqs.explain: Perceived behavioral control = confidence in one's ability to maintain (e.g.) a brushing routine.

mcqs.q: Social Cognitive Theory emphasises self-efficacy and:
mcqs.explain: Social Cognitive Theory: self-efficacy and role modeling influence how habits are adopted; children imitate parents or dental professionals.

mcqs.q: Patient compliance can be achieved through three factors:
mcqs.explain: Compliance can be achieved by cognitive (understanding), emotional (fear/motivation), and social (family/culture/peer) factors.

mcqs.q: The COGNITIVE compliance factor refers to:
opts: Understanding the importance of oral care
mcqs.explain: The cognitive factor = understanding the importance of oral care.

mcqs.q: ‘Fear of pain or motivation to avoid cavities’ is which compliance factor?
mcqs.explain: The emotional factor includes fear of pain or motivation to avoid cavities.

mcqs.q: According to the Health Belief Model, patients adopt preventive behavior when they perceive:
opts: A personal threat to their dental health
mcqs.explain: In the HBM, patients are more likely to act when they perceive a personal threat (e.g. risk of caries or periodontal disease).

mcqs.q: A second Health Belief Model condition is that the patient:
opts: Believes the recommended intervention is effective
mcqs.explain: The HBM also requires belief in the efficacy of the intervention (e.g. fluoride/brushing reduces risk).

mcqs.q: The third Health Belief Model condition is that the patient feels:
opts: Capable of overcoming barriers (financial, psychological, practical)
mcqs.explain: The HBM requires feeling capable of overcoming barriers — financial, psychological (e.g. anxiety), or practical (time/access).

mcqs.q: In the Health Belief Model, a school dental screening or a parent's reminder is an example of a:
mcqs.explain: Cues to action prompt behavior — e.g. a school dental screening or a parent's reminder prompting a child to brush.

mcqs.q: Regarding demographics in the HBM, studies show:
opts: Females may be more likely to seek preventive dental care than males
mcqs.explain: Demographics (gender): females may be more likely to seek preventive dental care than males.

mcqs.q: Which personality trait is linked to better adherence to oral hygiene?
mcqs.explain: Conscientious individuals often adhere better to oral hygiene routines.

mcqs.q: ‘Change can happen naturally in everyday life’ is illustrated by:
opts: A smoker quitting after his brother is hospitalised with lung disease
A dentist forcing a patient to change
A single piece of advice working instantly
mcqs.explain: Change can happen naturally — e.g. a chronic smoker stops after seeing his brother admitted with serious lung disease.

mcqs.q: Where and when does behavior change mainly occur?
opts: When the patient is ready, outside the dental clinic (over time)
mcqs.explain: Behavior change occurs when people are ready and outside the dental clinic — over a period, not immediately during treatment.

mcqs.q: A key limitation the clinician must understand is that:
opts: Advice alone has limits because of barriers like anxiety, beliefs and environment
mcqs.explain: There are limits to what advice alone can achieve because of barriers like anxiety, environmental/social factors, and underlying beliefs/values.

mcqs.q: The conversational environment that best supports change is:
opts: Warm, empathetic, respectful, with clear simple language
mcqs.explain: A warm, empathetic, respectful environment with clear simple language that is positive and encouraging has a significant positive impact.

mcqs.q: ‘Agreeing on priorities’ with the patient means:
opts: Involving the patient in decision-making and agreeing what is important
mcqs.explain: Agreeing on priorities = involving the patient in decision making and agreeing what is important to them.

saqs.q: Define compliance and non-compliance, and list three causes of non-compliance.
saqs.a: Compliance = the patient's behaviors match the provider's recommendations. Non-compliance = failure/refusal to comply. Causes (any 3): language barrier, low education, prioritising immediate pain relief, poor dentist–patient interaction, system barriers (financial, access, paperwork, inconvenient times).

The state of having mixed feelings or contradictory ideas about adopting/maintaining a behavior. The desire for good oral health is present, but perceived barriers & inconvenience create resistance — so the patient follows the behavior some days and not others.

saqs.q: List the five theories/mechanisms of behavior change.
saqs.a: 1) Foundations of health behavior change (intrinsic/extrinsic motivation + reinforcement), 2) Theory of Planned Behavior, 3) Social Cognitive Theory, 4) Patient compliance mechanisms, 5) The Health Belief Model.

saqs.q: Describe the Health Belief Model (its three core beliefs).
saqs.a: Patients adopt preventive behavior when they: 1) perceive a personal threat (risk of caries/perio), 2) believe the intervention is effective (e.g. fluoride/brushing reduces risk), and 3) feel capable of overcoming barriers (financial, psychological, practical). Modified by cues to action, demographics & personality.

saqs.q: Give the three components of the Theory of Planned Behavior.
saqs.a: Attitudes (belief in the value of the behavior), Social norms (others'/family expectations), and Perceived behavioral control (confidence in one's ability to maintain the behavior).

saqs.q: What can the clinician do to support behavior change?
saqs.a: Understand the limitations of giving advice; use good interpersonal skills in a warm, empathetic, respectful, simple, encouraging way; agree on priorities (involve the patient in decisions); and acknowledge ambivalence (accept ‘confused’ days, build trust, respect autonomy, listen actively, focus on the patient's own reasons).
